Lekha Singh 7 min read · Sep 21, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size When every decision makes sense on its own, the outcome can still miss the goal. I have been sitting through a lot of technology discussions lately, and one thing I have started noticing is that some of the most interesting ones do not really have a clearly right or wrong side. Engineering wants something reliable and maintainable. Product wants to solve the user problem without adding unnecessary complexity. The AI team wants to improve the quality of the output. Infrastructure is thinking about cost, scale, and what it will take to operate the system. Business is looking at timelines and what has been committed to the customer. And the interesting part is — everyone can be right. Each person can be making a completely sensible decision from where they are sitting. But when all those individually sensible decisions come together, the overall technology decision can still be wrong. That is something I had not really thought about before. I used to assume that if everyone was making a sensible decision from their own perspective, those decisions would eventually add up to a sensible overall answer. I am starting to realise that they do not always. Sometimes everyone is solving the same problem from a different angle. But sometimes, they are actually solving slightly different problems without even realising it. And I think that is where things get interesting. What are we actually optimising for? Take something as simple as choosing between two AI models. Imagine one performs at 93% on the metric we care about and another at 91%. It is very easy to look at that comparison and say that 93% is better. And on that metric, it is. But what if getting those additional two percentage points means significantly higher inference cost? What if the system becomes slower? What if it is much harder to retrain and operate? And what if most of that improvement happens in cases that barely affect the final decision made by the user? Suddenly, 93% and 91% are not enough information to make the decision. What do those additional two percentage points actually change? If they materially improve the outcome, the added complexity may be completely justified. If they do not, we may simply be improving the metric without improving the problem that actually matters. The same applies beyond AI. Lower cloud cost is valuable, unless achieving it creates a larger reliability problem. Faster delivery is valuable, unless every short-term decision creates another exception that somebody has to maintain later. More flexibility is useful, until the complexity required to support every possible case starts slowing everyone down. The trade-off is rarely between something good and something obviously bad. It is usually between things that are all valuable. Accuracy versus cost. Speed versus maintainability. Flexibility versus simplicity. Solving today’s requirement versus designing for something we may need tomorrow. So before asking which option is “best”, there is probably a more useful question. Best for what? Everyone can optimise their part and still make the whole thing worse This was probably the more surprising realisation for me. Suppose engineering optimises heavily for reliability and future scale. That sounds sensible. But perhaps the product is still being validated, and the expected scale is several years away. Now the team may spend much more time solving a future problem while slowing down what actually needs to be learned today. Or business optimises for getting something to the customer as quickly as possible. That is also sensible. But if every short-term commitment creates another exception in the underlying system, eventually engineering may spend more time managing those exceptions than building anything new. Infrastructure could successfully reduce cost. Product could successfully increase flexibility. AI could successfully improve model performance. Each function could do well against its own objective, and the complete system could still become more expensive, slower, or harder to change. I used to think trade-offs mainly showed up when people disagreed. Now I think that may actually be the easier case. The harder case is when everyone is right within their own frame. Then the question is not: Who has the better argument? It is: Are we actually optimising for the same outcome? Time changes what the right decision looks like There is another reason two people can look at exactly the same problem and reach completely different conclusions. They may simply be solving for different points in time. Imagine a customer needs a capability quickly. One option is to build exactly what is needed now. Another is to spend longer designing something generic enough to support several similar requirements in the future. Which one is the better engineering decision? There is not enough information yet. If this is genuinely a one-off requirement, the generic solution may simply be unnecessary complexity.
